topic: Day 1 · DKA Management I — Fluid Resuscitation
speakerTitle: Consultant in Intensive Care & Acute Medicine
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Unit
speakerBio: An intensivist who reminds every trainee that the first drug in DKA is salt water, and that the fastest way to harm a child in DKA is to resuscitate them too fast. Her rule: refill the tank, then respect the brain.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — 04:05, resus bay 2

The 19-year-old from Session 1 is now confirmed: pH 7.04, bicarbonate 6, BHB 6.8, glucose 31, potassium 4.9, and a systolic of 92 with a heart rate of 128. Her mouth is parched, her eyes sunken, her skin tents. The registrar reaches for the insulin. Stop his hand. In DKA the first and most powerful drug is not insulin — it is salt water. Restoring her circulating volume will drop her glucose before a single unit of insulin acts, protect her kidneys, and buy the time everything else depends on. This session is about getting the fluid right — and about the one fluid error that kills children.

1 · The one sentence that holds the session

In DKA, fluid comes first and fluid does more than you think. You are refilling a tank that has lost 5–7 litres — and just refilling it drops the glucose, restores the kidney, and reverses the vicious cycle before insulin even arrives.

2 · The deficit — how dry is this patient, really? 💧

By the time DKA is established the osmotic diuresis (Session 1) has produced a staggering deficit:

  • Water: ~100 mL/kg — in a 70 kg adult that is ~7 litres; typical range 5–7 L.
  • Sodium: 7–10 mmol/kg. Potassium: 3–5 mmol/kg (Session 4). Also chloride, phosphate and magnesium.

This is not a patient who is "a bit dry". This is a patient who has lost more than a tenth of their body weight in water, and whose circulation is running on the fumes of sympathetic vasoconstriction. That is why fluid, not insulin, is the resuscitation.

💡 Pearl — fluid drops the glucose before insulin acts

Restoring circulating volume lowers blood glucose by two mechanisms independent of insulin: (1) dilution of the glucose in an expanded plasma volume, and (2) — the big one — restoring renal perfusion and GFR, so the kidney resumes excreting glucose in the urine. Studies show a substantial fall in glucose from fluids alone in the first hour or two. This is the vicious cycle of Session 1 running backwards: more volume → better GFR → more glucosuria → lower glucose → less osmotic diuresis. Fluid is the first hypoglycaemic agent in DKA.

3 · The fluid of choice — isotonic 0.9% saline 🧂

First-line resuscitation fluid in DKA (JBDS-IP) is 0.9% sodium chloride (isotonic saline). Why isotonic crystalloid?

  • The primary deficit is of isotonic salt and water lost through the osmotic diuresis — you replace like with like.
  • It expands the intravascular volume to restore perfusion, without dropping serum osmolality abruptly (which risks fluid shifting into the brain — see cerebral oedema below).
  • It is cheap, universally available, and its potassium can be added directly to the bag.
🎯 0.9% saline vs balanced crystalloids

Large-volume 0.9% saline can produce a hyperchloraemic (normal-anion-gap) metabolic acidosis, which can blunt the rise in bicarbonate and confuse your monitoring — which is exactly why JBDS emphasises tracking ketones (BHB) and the anion gap rather than bicarbonate alone. Some centres and the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus note that balanced solutions (e.g. Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte) may resolve DKA slightly faster and cause less hyperchloraemia. Both are acceptable; 0.9% saline remains the standard first-line, and consistency plus careful potassium management matters more than the choice between them.

4 · The JBDS fluid regimen — fast first, then slow 📉

The principle is rapid replacement of circulating volume first, then a slower, steady replacement of the remaining deficit over the next day. A representative JBDS-style regimen for a haemodynamically stable adult (systolic ≥90) with normal renal and cardiac function:

FluidVolumeOver
0.9% saline1000 mL1st hour (no potassium in this first bag)
0.9% saline + KCl1000 mLnext 2 hours
0.9% saline + KCl1000 mLnext 2 hours
0.9% saline + KCl1000 mLnext 4 hours
0.9% saline + KCl1000 mLnext 4 hours
0.9% saline + KCl1000 mLnext 6 hours

Read the rhythm: 1 L in 1 h → 1 L in 2 h → 1 L in 2 h → 1 L in 4 h → 1 L in 4 h → 1 L in 6 h. The intervals lengthen as you move from resuscitating the circulation to replacing the deficit gently. For the shocked patient (systolic <90) give a 500 mL bolus over 10–15 minutes first and reassess, repeating up to ~1–2 L, then join the regimen; if the systolic stays below 90 after ~1 L, escalate to senior/critical-care review and consider another cause.

⚠️ Danger — the "no potassium in the first bag" rule

The first litre contains no potassium — it goes in fast before you have the potassium result. But every subsequent bag must have potassium added according to the serum level, because insulin and correction of acidosis will drive potassium into cells and the level will fall (Session 4). Give the first bag stat, get the potassium, and never run bag two without it addressed. Fluids and potassium are inseparable in DKA.

5 · Corrected sodium — the number that warns you of danger ⚠️

Sodium behaves counter-intuitively in DKA, and understanding it is what keeps you safe. Glucose is osmotically active: high plasma glucose pulls water out of cells into the plasma, diluting the measured sodium (a "translocational" or dilutional pseudohyponatraemia). So the measured sodium reads low while the true, water-corrected sodium may be normal or high.

Estimate the corrected sodium: add ~2.4 mmol/L to the measured sodium for every 5.5 mmol/L that glucose is above 5.5. (US units: add ~1.6–2.4 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100.)

As treatment proceeds…Expected / safeWorrying
Measured sodiumRises as glucose falls (water returns into cells)Fails to rise / falls sharply
Corrected sodiumStays stable or rises modestlyFalls → osmolality is dropping too fast
💡 Pearl — a falling corrected sodium is your cerebral-oedema alarm

As glucose falls with treatment, the measured sodium should rise — this is normal and reassuring, reflecting water moving back into cells as the osmotic pull of glucose eases. What you fear is the opposite: a falling corrected sodium, which signals that plasma osmolality is dropping too rapidly. A rapid osmolar fall pulls water into the brain and is the setup for cerebral oedema. Track corrected sodium: it should climb gently as glucose comes down. If it is falling, slow the osmolar shift — slow the glucose fall, slow the fluids.

6 · When to add 10% dextrose 🍬

Here is a point that confuses trainees: you add glucose to a hyperglycaemic patient. Once the blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (~250 mg/dL), start 10% dextrose (e.g. 125 mL/h) alongside the saline — while continuing the fixed-rate insulin. Why? Because the insulin is there to clear the ketones, not the glucose (Session 4), and it must keep running until the ketoacidosis resolves. If you let the glucose fall too low without dextrose you would have to stop the insulin — and the ketogenesis would restart. Dextrose lets you keep insulin running to finish clearing the ketones without causing hypoglycaemia. This bridges directly into Session 4.

Add 10% dextrose at glucose <14 mmol/L not to feed the patient but to protect the insulin infusion — the infusion that is still burning off the acid.

7 · Cautious fluids — who you must NOT flood 🚸

The standard regimen assumes a young, previously well, haemodynamically stable adult. Several groups need slower, more cautious, closely monitored fluid replacement:

GroupRiskApproach
Children & young adults (<25 y, esp. <18)Cerebral oedema — rare but frequently fatal; the leading cause of DKA death in childrenFollow paediatric DKA (BSPED) protocols; slower, weight-calculated fluids; avoid rapid osmolar shifts; neuro-obs.
ElderlyFluid overload, pulmonary oedemaSlower rates, frequent reassessment, consider monitoring of fluid status.
Heart failure / cardiac diseasePulmonary oedema from aggressive volumesCautious, titrated fluids; senior input; watch for crepitations, hypoxia.
Renal impairmentOverload; and potassium handling is alteredCareful fluid and potassium titration; senior/renal input.
PregnancyBoth mother and foetus at risk; ketoacidosis poorly toleratedPrompt but monitored resuscitation, obstetric involvement, foetal monitoring.
⚠️ Danger — cerebral oedema in children

Cerebral oedema is the most feared complication of DKA and is chiefly a disease of children and young people. It carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. Risk is linked to the severity of the acidosis/dehydration and, importantly, to over-rapid fluid administration and over-rapid falls in glucose and osmolality. Warning signs — headache, irritability, falling GCS, bradycardia with rising BP (Cushing's response), incontinence — typically appear 4–12 hours into treatment. Treatment is urgent: hypertonic saline or mannitol, slow the fluids, and get critical care and paediatrics involved immediately. Prevention is the same message as the corrected-sodium pearl: do not drop the osmolality too fast.

☠️ M&M — "We just wanted to catch her up"

A 14-year-old girl presented in severe DKA (pH 6.98, glucose 34). Keen to correct her rapidly, the team ran two litres of saline as fast boluses in the first hour and drove her glucose from 34 to 9 mmol/L within three hours. Six hours in she developed a headache, then became drowsy and bradycardic with a rising blood pressure. A CT confirmed cerebral oedema; despite mannitol and intubation she was left with a permanent neurological deficit. The retrospective was painful: her fluids were given faster than a paediatric protocol allows, no 10% dextrose was added as the glucose fell, and the osmolality — and corrected sodium — dropped precipitously, pulling water into a vulnerable young brain. Lessons: (1) in children and young people, resuscitate briskly for shock but otherwise replace the deficit slowly per paediatric protocols; (2) do not race the glucose down — add 10% dextrose at <14 mmol/L; (3) watch the corrected sodium and neuro-obs; a falling corrected sodium and a headache in an adolescent with DKA is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise. Speed felt like care; it caused harm.

8 · Take-home 🎯

  • The DKA fluid deficit is ~100 mL/kg (often 5–7 L) — this patient is profoundly, not mildly, dry.
  • Fluid comes first and is itself a hypoglycaemic agent — restoring GFR resumes glucosuria and drops glucose before insulin acts, reversing the vicious cycle.
  • First-line fluid is 0.9% saline (balanced crystalloids are a reasonable alternative); regimen is fast first (1 L in 1 h) then progressively slower.
  • No potassium in the first bag; potassium in every bag thereafter, guided by the level.
  • Watch the corrected sodium: measured Na should rise as glucose falls; a falling corrected sodium warns of over-rapid osmolar shift and cerebral oedema.
  • Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 mmol/L to keep the insulin running for ketone clearance.
  • Cautious fluids in the young (cerebral oedema), elderly, cardiac and renal patients. Do not drop osmolality too fast.

Next session: the second pillar — insulin and ketone clearance. The fixed-rate infusion, why you keep the basal insulin running, the targets that tell you it is working, and the rebound DKA that follows when insulin is stopped too soon.

moderatorQs.q: A registrar wants to reach straight for insulin in a shocked DKA patient with a systolic of 88. Why is fluid, not insulin, the correct first move — and what does the fluid achieve that insulin does not?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because this patient is dying of volume depletion — a 5–7 litre deficit — and the immediate threat is circulatory collapse and organ hypoperfusion, which insulin does nothing to fix and can worsen. Fluid does several things insulin cannot: it restores circulating volume and blood pressure, it restores renal perfusion and GFR so the kidney resumes excreting glucose and ketones, and through dilution plus renal clearance it drops the glucose substantially before insulin even acts — running the Session 1 vicious cycle backwards. Give a 500 mL 0.9% saline bolus over 10–15 minutes and reassess, repeating up to 1–2 L for a systolic below 90, escalating to critical care if it stays below 90. Crucially, starting insulin before fluids also risks a dangerous potassium shift into a still-depleted patient. So: fill the tank first, then insulin to clear the ketones.

moderatorQs.q: As you treat a DKA, the laboratory sodium is rising from 132 to 141. A junior is alarmed. Why is this usually reassuring, and what sodium trend would actually worry you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A rising measured sodium as the glucose falls is normal and reassuring. At presentation the high glucose was osmotically pulling water out of cells into the plasma, diluting the measured sodium (translocational pseudohyponatraemia). As treatment lowers the glucose, that water moves back into cells and the measured sodium rises toward its true value — expected physiology, not iatrogenic hypernatraemia. What should genuinely worry you is the opposite: a falling corrected sodium (measured Na corrected upward by ~2.4 mmol/L per 5.5 mmol/L of glucose above normal). A falling corrected sodium means plasma osmolality is dropping too fast, which draws water into the brain and is the physiological setup for cerebral oedema. So: measured Na rising = good; corrected Na falling = slow the osmolar shift, slow the glucose fall and the fluids, and watch the neurology.

moderatorQs.q: Why, and at what point, do you add 10% dextrose to a patient whose glucose is still elevated — and what would go wrong if you didn't?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: You add 10% dextrose once the blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (~250 mg/dL), running it alongside the saline. The logic is that in DKA the insulin infusion exists to clear the ketoacidosis, not the glucose — and it must keep running at a fixed rate until the ketones and acidosis resolve (BHB <0.6, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15). But glucose typically normalises well before the ketones do. If you had no dextrose, you would be forced to either stop the insulin (letting ketogenesis restart) or push the patient into hypoglycaemia. Adding 10% dextrose lets you keep the fixed-rate insulin running safely to finish burning off the ketones without hypoglycaemia. Omitting it is a classic error that either stalls ketone clearance or causes a dangerous hypo.

audienceQs.q: The regimen says no potassium in the first litre but potassium in every bag after. Why the difference?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because of timing and safety. The first litre goes in fast (over an hour) as resuscitation, usually before the potassium result is back — and giving potassium blind, quickly, to a patient whose admission potassium might be high (acidosis and insulin lack push K⁺ out of cells, so the serum level is often normal or elevated at presentation) risks dangerous hyperkalaemia. So the first bag is plain 0.9% saline, run stat. By the second bag you have the potassium level, and now the priority reverses: once you start insulin and correct the acidosis, potassium is driven into cells and the serum level falls, on a background of severe total-body depletion. So every subsequent bag has potassium added according to the level (typically 40 mmol/L when K⁺ is 3.5–5.5 with urine output; withhold and recheck if above 5.5 or anuric). In short: first bag fast and plain; thereafter, replace potassium to stay ahead of insulin's shift.

audienceQs.q: We have an 82-year-old man with DKA and a history of heart failure. Should I be running the same fast fluids I would for a young patient?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — he needs slower, more cautious, closely monitored fluids. The standard 'fast-first' regimen assumes a young, previously well heart that can handle rapid large volumes. In an elderly patient with heart failure, the same rates risk tipping him into pulmonary oedema. He still needs his deficit corrected because DKA must be treated, but you do it more gently: smaller/slower boluses only for genuine shock, longer intervals between bags, and frequent reassessment for fluid overload — new crepitations at the lung bases, rising respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturations, raised JVP. Get senior review early, monitor urine output and fluid balance carefully, and don't hesitate to slow the rate if he shows signs of overload. The same caution applies to patients with renal impairment. Escalate rather than run a standard protocol on autopilot in these groups.

audienceQs.q: Why is everyone so much more careful with fluids in children with DKA than in adults?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because in children and young people the great danger of DKA is cerebral oedema — rare, but the leading cause of DKA death in that age group, with high rates of death and permanent neurological injury. The developing brain is more vulnerable to rapid shifts in osmolality, and cerebral oedema is associated with the severity of the illness and with over-rapid fluid administration and over-rapid falls in glucose/osmolality. So paediatric protocols (e.g. BSPED) use carefully weight-calculated, slower fluid replacement, cautious boluses reserved for true shock, and deliberate avoidance of racing the glucose down (adding dextrose as it falls). The team watches closely for warning signs 4–12 hours in — headache, irritability, falling conscious level, bradycardia with rising blood pressure — and treats suspected cerebral oedema immediately with hypertonic saline or mannitol and critical care. In short: adults tolerate brisk correction far better; in children, too fast is the thing that kills.
